text.p: VIENNA, July 25 (Reuter) The main stories in the Austrian press this Friday are:
DIE PRESSE
- Austria's proposed double budget for 1998 and 1999 causes painful cuts in early pensions and the civil service.
- Economic research institute IHS says the government's savings measures are holding back the economy.

- Troubles at sporting goods unit HTM throw a cloud over the flotation of Austria Tabak, planned for October. Austria Tabak is currently checking whether it would get back its 1.2 billion schilling dowry in the event of HTM's bankruptcy.
DER STANDARD
- Finance Minister Edlinger says the state deficit will decline from 1999 onwards.
- The budget's immediate measures should bring the state 16 billion schillings.
- HTM is prepared to offer part of the company's shares as security for loans from creditor banks of around two billion schillings.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN
- European Union expansion could cost Austria eight billion schillings, says SPOe Euro MP Herbert Boesch.
- Extreme mountain climber Tirolean Reinhold Messner claims to have found the Yeti, according to magazine News.
- The Bayerishe Hypo- and Vereinsbank sees big chances for the future in the Austrian market.
- The three regional banks Oberbank, BKS and BTV say they are not for sale.
- Banks set HTM an ultimatum. Action is demanded.
KURIER
- There has been more rain in Austria this July than in any July since 1897.
- The high dollar could create 750,000 jobs in Europe, 15,000 of them in Austria, estimates the Institute for Higher Studies.
- 37 percent of Austrians expect a better development of the economy, up from 29 percent a year ago, according to a Fessel & Gfk poll.
- The Austrian Federal Economic Chamber has welcomed the eastwards expansion of the EU, but expects problems on border controls.
WIENER ZEITUNG
- The coalition partners agreed their double budget for 1998 and 1999. It predicts a deficit of 67.3 billion schillings in 1998 and of 70.1 billion schillings in 1999.
- An ACNielsen poll finds that 21% of Austrians make use of extending shopping times beyond 18.30 every week.
